title: Emission and absorption of infrared radiation

notes.definition: All bodies (objects), no matter what their temperature, emit and absorb infrared radiation. The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time.
explanation: Every object emits infrared radiation, whatever its temperature. An ice cube, your body, a cup of tea and the Sun all emit infrared. Every object also absorbs infrared radiation from its surroundings. Infrared is an electromagnetic wave, so it can travel through a vacuum: this is how energy from the Sun reaches the Earth, and why you feel warm in front of a fire even though the air between you and the fire is not doing the heating.

The hotter an object is, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time. A cup of tea at 80 °C emits infrared at a much greater rate than the same cup at room temperature. This is why infrared cameras (thermal imaging cameras) can show differences in temperature: hotter objects emit more infrared and appear brighter in the image. It also explains why a hot object cools down: it emits more infrared than it absorbs from its cooler surroundings.

Whether an object warms up or cools down depends on the balance between the infrared it absorbs and the infrared it emits. An object that absorbs more infrared than it emits gets hotter. An object that emits more than it absorbs cools down. An object at the same temperature as its surroundings absorbs and emits at the same rate, so its temperature stays constant.

The type of surface also affects how much infrared is emitted and absorbed. Dark, matt surfaces are good emitters and good absorbers of infrared. Light, shiny surfaces are poor emitters and poor absorbers; they are good reflectors of infrared. A good emitter is always a good absorber. This is investigated using a Leslie cube in required practical 10 (covered with properties of electromagnetic waves). For the same surface, the hotter it is, the more infrared it emits.

These ideas explain many everyday design choices. Radiators and the cooling fins on engines are often painted dark so they emit more infrared. Kettles and teapots may be shiny so they emit less and keep drinks hot. Emergency blankets are shiny to reduce infrared emitted by the casualty. Solar water-heating panels are matt black to absorb as much infrared from the Sun as possible.
keyFacts: All bodies emit and absorb infrared radiation, whatever their temperature.
The hotter a body, the more infrared it radiates in a given time.
Infrared is an EM wave and can travel through a vacuum.
An object warms up if it absorbs infrared faster than it emits it.
An object cools down if it emits infrared faster than it absorbs it.
At constant temperature, absorption and emission rates are equal.
Matt black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers of infrared.
Shiny, light surfaces are poor emitters and absorbers but good reflectors.
Thermal imaging cameras detect the infrared emitted by objects.

keyTerms.definition: Electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths longer than visible light, emitted and absorbed by all objects.
To take in radiation, transferring its energy to the object's internal energy.
The amount of radiation emitted in a given time.
A camera that forms an image from the infrared emitted by objects, showing temperature differences.
A surface, such as matt black, that emits a lot of infrared at a given temperature; it is also a good absorber.

workedExamples.title: Explaining cooling
workedExamples.question: A mug of hot chocolate at 70 °C is left in a room at 20 °C. Explain, in terms of infrared radiation, why it cools down.
steps: The mug emits infrared radiation and also absorbs infrared from the room.
Because the mug is hotter than the room, it emits infrared at a greater rate than it absorbs it.
There is a net transfer of energy away from the mug, so its temperature falls.
As it cools, it emits less infrared in a given time, so it cools more slowly until it reaches room temperature.
workedExamples.answer: It emits more infrared than it absorbs, so it loses energy and cools, more slowly as its temperature falls.

workedExamples.title: Interpreting a thermal image
workedExamples.question: A thermal image of a house in winter shows the windows much brighter than the walls. What does this show?
steps: Brighter areas in a thermal image emit more infrared.
Hotter surfaces emit more infrared in a given time.
So the windows are warmer on the outside than the walls: more energy is being lost through the windows.
workedExamples.answer: The windows are hotter, so more energy is escaping through them than through the walls.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think only hot objects emit infrared.
misconceptions.right: In fact all objects emit infrared, whatever their temperature; colder objects just emit less in a given time.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think cold objects 'give out cold'.
misconceptions.right: In fact cold objects absorb more infrared than they emit; there is no such thing as 'cold' radiation.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a shiny surface is a good emitter because it is bright.
misconceptions.right: In fact shiny surfaces are poor emitters and poor absorbers of infrared; they are good reflectors.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think an object at constant temperature has stopped emitting infrared.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is still emitting, but it absorbs infrared at the same rate.

realWorld: Thermal imaging cameras help firefighters find people in smoke and help surveyors find heat loss from buildings.
Solar water-heating panels are painted matt black to absorb as much infrared as possible.
Shiny emergency blankets reduce the infrared emitted by a casualty, keeping them warm.
Night-vision cameras detect the infrared emitted by animals for wildlife filming.
separateOnlyContent: This subtopic is in separate Physics only: all bodies emit and absorb infrared radiation, and the hotter the body, the more infrared it radiates in a given time.
examTips: Use the phrase 'in a given time' when describing how much infrared a hotter object emits.
Remember all objects emit infrared: never say a cold object emits none.
To explain warming or cooling, compare the rate of absorption with the rate of emission.
Link surface type to emission: matt black is the best emitter and absorber, shiny silver the worst.
Do not confuse infrared radiation with conduction or convection; radiation needs no medium.
summary: All objects emit and absorb infrared radiation.
Hotter objects emit more infrared in a given time.
Warming: absorb faster than emit. Cooling: emit faster than absorb.
Matt black: best emitter and absorber. Shiny: poor emitter and absorber.

flashcards.back: The hotter the object, the more infrared it emits in a given time.
Yes, but less in a given time than hotter objects.

flashcards.front: When does an object's temperature increase?
flashcards.back: When it absorbs infrared faster than it emits it.

flashcards.front: When does an object's temperature stay constant?
flashcards.back: When it absorbs and emits infrared at the same rate.

flashcards.front: Good emitters of infrared are also...
Can infrared travel through a vacuum?
flashcards.back: Yes; it is an electromagnetic wave.

flashcards.front: How does a thermal imaging camera work?
flashcards.back: It detects infrared emitted by objects; hotter objects emit more and appear brighter.

flashcards.front: Why are solar panels for heating water matt black?

flashcards.front: Why does a hot drink cool down?

questions.question: Which objects emit infrared radiation?
markScheme: 1 mark: All objects, whatever their temperature
questions.explanation: All bodies emit and absorb infrared, no matter what their temperature.

questions.question: Which type of surface is the best emitter of infrared radiation?
markScheme: 1 mark: Matt black
questions.explanation: Matt black surfaces are the best emitters (and absorbers) of infrared.

questions.question:
An object gets hotter.
What happens to the amount of infrared radiation it emits in a given time?
markScheme: 1 mark: It increases
questions.explanation: The hotter the body, the more infrared it radiates in a given time.

questions.question:
An ice cube is at −10 °C.
Which statement is correct?
options: It emits no infrared because it is cold
It emits and absorbs infrared radiation
It absorbs infrared but cannot emit it
markScheme: 1 mark: It emits and absorbs infrared radiation
questions.explanation: All objects emit and absorb infrared. The ice cube emits less than warmer objects.

questions.question:
The temperature of an object is increasing.
Which statement must be true?
options: It is emitting infrared faster than it is absorbing it
It is absorbing infrared faster than it is emitting it
It is absorbing and emitting at the same rate
markScheme: 1 mark: It is absorbing infrared faster than it is emitting it
questions.explanation: A net gain of energy by radiation means absorption is faster than emission.

questions.question:
The outside of a teapot is sometimes made shiny.
What is the reason for this?
options: Shiny surfaces absorb more infrared from the room
Shiny surfaces emit more infrared, keeping the tea hot
Shiny surfaces are poor emitters, so less energy is lost by infrared
markScheme: 1 mark: Shiny surfaces are poor emitters, so less energy is lost by infrared
questions.explanation: Shiny surfaces emit little infrared, so the tea stays hot for longer.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows two identical cans. One can is matt black and the other is shiny silver.
Both cans are filled with water at 80 °C.
Which statement is correct?

options: The black can cools faster because it emits infrared at a greater rate
The shiny can cools faster because it reflects more infrared
Both cool at the same rate because they start at the same temperature
The black can stays hot longer because it absorbs more infrared
markScheme: 1 mark: The black can cools faster because it emits infrared at a greater rate
questions.explanation: At the same temperature, the matt black can emits more infrared per second. Although it also absorbs more, its surroundings are cooler, so its net loss is larger.

questions.question:
A thermal imaging camera shows a person as brighter than the wall behind them.
What can be concluded?
options: The wall is not emitting any infrared
The person is reflecting visible light
The person is emitting more infrared in a given time, so is hotter than the wall
The wall is absorbing all of the infrared from the person
markScheme: 1 mark: The person is emitting more infrared in a given time, so is hotter than the wall
questions.explanation: Brightness in a thermal image indicates more infrared emitted. The wall still emits infrared, just less.

questions.question: How is energy from the Sun transferred to the Earth through space?
options: By infrared and other EM radiation, which can travel through a vacuum
markScheme: 1 mark: By infrared and other EM radiation, which can travel through a vacuum
questions.explanation: Space is a vacuum, so conduction and convection cannot occur. EM radiation needs no medium.

questions.question:
The temperature of an object increases.
What happens to the rate at which the object emits infrared radiation?
markScheme: 1 mark: it increases / more infrared is emitted in a given time
questions.explanation: Hotter objects emit more infrared per second.

1 mark: so more energy from the Sun is transferred to the water, heating it more
questions.explanation: Good absorbers increase the energy transferred from sunlight.

questions.question:
A car is left in the sun on a hot day.
Explain why the car gets hotter and then reaches a steady temperature.
markScheme: 1 mark: at first it absorbs infrared faster than it emits, so its temperature rises
1 mark: as it gets hotter it emits more, until emission equals absorption and the temperature stays constant
questions.explanation: Emission rises with temperature until the two rates balance.

questions.question:
Marathon runners are given shiny emergency blankets at the end of a race.
Suggest and explain why the blankets are shiny.
markScheme: 1 mark: shiny surfaces are poor emitters of infrared
1 mark: so less energy is lost from the blanket's outer surface by radiation
1 mark: the inner shiny surface also reflects infrared emitted by the runner back towards them, keeping them warm
questions.explanation: Shiny surfaces reduce radiation losses in both ways.

questions.question:
A student makes this statement.
'An object at the same temperature as its surroundings does not emit any infrared radiation.'
Explain why the student is wrong.
acceptedAnswers: emits and absorbs at same rate
markScheme: 1 mark: all objects emit infrared whatever their temperature
1 mark: it absorbs infrared at the same rate as it emits it, so its temperature stays constant
questions.explanation: Constant temperature means balanced rates, not zero emission.

questions.question: Name a device that forms an image from the infrared radiation emitted by objects.
markScheme: 1 mark: thermal imaging camera / infrared camera
questions.explanation: Infrared cameras show warmer objects as brighter.

questions.question: Describe how the temperature of an object and the type of its surface affect the infrared radiation the object emits.
markScheme: Indicative content:
all objects emit infrared whatever their temperature
the hotter the object, the more infrared it emits in a given time
matt black surfaces emit the most infrared
shiny silver / light shiny surfaces emit the least
dark surfaces emit more than light; matt more than shiny
good emitters are also good absorbers
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of both temperature and surface effects.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one factor described simply.
questions.explanation: Both the temperature and the surface affect the rate of emission.

questions.question:
A householder wants to keep a hot water tank hot.
The householder also wants a radiator to warm a room quickly.
Explain what type of surface should be used for the tank and for the radiator.
Explain how the temperature of each object affects the infrared radiation it emits.
markScheme: Indicative content:
all objects emit and absorb infrared; hotter objects emit more in a given time
hot water tank is hotter than the room so it emits more than it absorbs and cools
tank should have a shiny / light surface: poor emitter, so less energy lost by radiation
radiator should be matt black / dark: good emitter, so more infrared emitted per second to warm the room
the hotter the radiator, the more infrared it emits
as the tank cools, it emits less, so cooling slows
objects reach constant temperature when absorption and emission rates are equal
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct surfaces for both with clear explanations linked to emission, and correct effect of temperature.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct surface for both or one with good explanation; some reference to temperature.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about surfaces or temperature.
questions.explanation: Choose poor emitters to keep things hot and good emitters to transfer energy away quickly.

questions.question: Which type of surface is the best absorber of infrared radiation?
markScheme: 1 mark: Matt black
questions.explanation: Good emitters are good absorbers, so matt black absorbs most.

questions.question: What type of wave is infrared radiation?
markScheme: 1 mark: Electromagnetic
questions.explanation: Infrared is part of the electromagnetic spectrum, between microwaves and visible light.

questions.question:
An object stays at a constant temperature.
Which statement is correct?
options: It absorbs and emits infrared at the same rate
It neither absorbs nor emits infrared
markScheme: 1 mark: It absorbs and emits infrared at the same rate
questions.explanation: Constant temperature means no net energy change: absorption and emission rates balance.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the temperatures of two identical metal blocks.
The blocks are placed in the same room.
Which statement is correct?
options: Both blocks emit the same amount of infrared because they are the same material
Block A emits much more infrared each second than block B
Block B emits more infrared because it absorbs more
markScheme: 1 mark: Block A emits much more infrared each second than block B
questions.explanation: Both blocks emit infrared, because all objects do. Block A is much hotter (300 °C), so it emits much more infrared radiation in a given time than block B (30 °C).

questions.question:
The radiators used to cool car engines are often painted black.
What is the main reason for this?
options: Black surfaces emit infrared at a greater rate, transferring energy away faster
Black surfaces reflect infrared back into the engine
Black surfaces absorb energy from the engine by convection
markScheme: 1 mark: Black surfaces emit infrared at a greater rate, transferring energy away faster
questions.explanation: A good emitter transfers more energy away from the hot radiator by infrared each second.

questions.question: What is meant by a good absorber of infrared radiation?
acceptedAnswers: absorbs a large proportion of infrared falling on it
markScheme: 1 mark: a surface that absorbs most of the infrared radiation falling on it (reflects little)
questions.explanation: Matt black surfaces are good absorbers.

questions.question:
Two identical cups of tea at 80 °C are placed outside.
One cup is outside on a cold day. The other cup is outside on a warm day.
Table 1 shows the air temperature on each day.
Explain which cup of tea cools faster.
acceptedAnswers: bigger difference between emission and absorption
markScheme: 1 mark: the cup on the cold day cools faster
1 mark: it absorbs less infrared from the colder surroundings, so the difference between emission and absorption (net loss) is greater
questions.explanation: Both cups emit at the same rate at 80 °C; what differs is how much they absorb.

the object emits and absorbs infrared at all times
